Preferences are remembered for the user across launches and across all projects, in the platform's per-user config directory, never in a project.

- the recent projects
- the folder a project was last opened from
- the harness runs go to, which starts as Claude Code

A preference that can't be saved still holds for the rest of the session. Only light or dark mode says so, as the commands that change it do; the others, brightness and the chosen colours among them, fail quietly, being only a convenience.

Shown in an [InsetPanelScope](../../ui/components/inset-panel/index.md#inset-panel-scope) over the main window, not a window of its own. It is headed "Settings", with a close button whose tooltip says it closes the settings; closing the panel any way an inset panel closes closes them too.

#### Sidebar

Beneath the heading, down its left, a sidebar of vertical tabs, one per section, in order: "System prompts", "Injected prompts", "Agent", and "Containers". Each tab is a row across the sidebar's width reading the section's name, and the one picked is marked with the theme's accent. Clicking a tab picks its section, and the page beside the sidebar shows only that section, scrolled back to its top. The sidebar is a fixed 180 pixels wide, with a thin line down its right edge where it meets the page. "System prompts" is picked when the application starts, and the section picked stays picked while 
The page fills the rest of the width, and scrolls with a [ScrollbarScope](../../ui/components/scrollbar/index.md#scrollbar-scope).

#### Opening

It opens with Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS) from anywhere in the application, or from whatever command opens the settings, in place of anything else in the inset panel. Opening it while it is already open leaves it as it is rather than opening another.

#### System Prompts
#### Agent

The "Agent" section is headed "Agent", with a muted line beneath saying that every run, the tasks, the questions, and the application's own, goes to the harness picked here, and that a conversation is only carried on by the harness it began with.
Then a row for each harness, in order: Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode, each a radio button reading its name, with the command it runs muted beside it, `claude`, `codex`, or `opencode`, and "Not installed" muted after that when the command can't be found. use /lib
from /scope/application/MainWindow import MainWindowScope
from /scope/edge-releases import EdgeReleasesScope
from /scope/settings-window import SettingsWindowScope
from /scope/user-preferences import UserPreferencesScope

export scope SelfUpdateScope:
    concept: {SelfUpdateConcept}

concept SelfUpdateConcept:
    pitch:
        Suspense keeps itself up to date: it looks for a newer edge release,
        downloads it in the background, and puts it in place of its own
        binary when it restarts, so the newest build is only a restart away.

    shape: {SelfUpdateShape}

shape SelfUpdateShape:
    description:
        Updates come from the edge releases, as the @{EdgeReleasesScope}
        says, published in the GitHub repository the running build was
        published from, which it knows because that is baked into it. Only
        such a build updates itself. A build made anywhere else, as on a
        developer's machine, never looks for an update, never downloads one,
        and never replaces its binary, and the Updates section says why.

    checking:
        A check asks GitHub's releases API for the repository's releases,
        pre-releases included, and takes the one with the highest version
        `0.1.N`, comparing N as a number, never as text. It is newer only
        when its N is greater than the running build's; an older or equal one
        is never taken, so an update never goes back. A release without the
        asset for the running platform is passed over for the newest one
        that has it.

        Suspense checks a few seconds after it starts, and then every 6
        hours while it runs, in the background, never holding up anything
        else, and only while "Check for updates automatically" is on, as it
        is until turned off. That choice is remembered for the user, as the
        @{UserPreferencesScope} says. Check for updates, in the Updates
        section, checks straight away, whether it is on or not. A check that
        can't be made, as with no network or GitHub refusing it, is quiet
        when automatic, trying again at the next, and says why when asked
        for.

    downloading:

        background: the asset for the platform and architecture running,

use /lib
from /scope/application import ApplicationScope

export scope EdgeReleasesScope:
    concept: {EdgeReleasesConcept}

concept EdgeReleasesConcept:
    pitch:
        Every commit that lands on main is built for Linux, Windows, and
        macOS, and published on GitHub as an edge release anyone can
        download, so the newest Suspense is always one download away.

    shape: {EdgeReleasesShape}

shape EdgeReleasesShape:
    description:
        A GitHub Actions workflow in this application's own repository,
        `.github/workflows/edge.yml`, builds and publishes an edge release
        for each push to its `main` branch, and for nothing else: not pull
        requests, not other branches, and not tags. It runs once per push,
        for the commit at its head. Edge releases are nightly-like builds of
        whatever main holds, not stable releases, and are marked as such.

    version:
        An edge release's version is `0.1.N`, where N is the commit's
        sequence number on main: how many commits its history holds,
        counted by `git rev-list --count` on that commit, so each commit on
        main has its own number, one more than its parent's, and the same
        commit always gets the same version. The workflow checks out the
        whole history to count it, never a shallow clone.

        The version is baked into the binary when it is built, so the
        application knows its own version. A build made anywhere else, as
        on a developer's machine, has the version Cargo.toml gives it.

    builds:
        The application is built in release mode, one job per platform, run
        side by side, each on a GitHub-hosted runner of that platform:

        - Linux, x86_64, on Ubuntu
        - Windows, x86_64
        - macOS, Apple silicon, aarch64

        Each job runs the project's tests before building, and installs
        whatever the platform needs to build the application's GUI, as
        Linux's windowing and font libraries. Each builds from the
        repository as it is at that commit, the default prompts in
        `.suspense/system-prompts` included, as the application's build
        needs them. The Windows binary is a GUI application, opening no
        console of its own, as the @{ApplicationScope} says.

    publishing:
        Once every platform's job has succeeded, one GitHub release is
        published for the commit, tagged `v0.1.N` on that commit, titled
        "Suspense 0.1.N (edge)", and marked as a pre-release, never as the
        latest stable release. Its notes give the commit's short hash,
        linked to the commit, and its message's first line.

        Its assets are one archive per platform, each holding the binary
        alone, named for the version and the platform:

        - `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`
        - `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip`
        - `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`

        The binaries are not signed or notarized.

        If any platform's job fails, nothing is published for that commit,
        so no edge release ever lacks a platform; the workflow run shows
        which job failed. A release already published for a version, as when
        a run is re-run, is never published twice: the run publishes nothing
        more for it and succeeds.

        Pushes are handled in the order they came: a run waits for the one
        before it to finish rather than cancelling it, so every commit on
        main gets its edge release. The workflow is given only the
        permission it needs to publish, writing the repository's contents,
        and uses the token GitHub gives each run, needing no secrets of its
        own.

concept SelfUpdateConcept:
    pitch:
        Suspense keeps itself up to date: it looks for a newer edge release,
        downloads it in the background, and puts it in place of its own
        binary when it restarts, so the newest build is only a restart away.

    shape: {SelfUpdateShape}

shape SelfUpdateShape:
    description:
        Updates come from the edge releases, as the @{EdgeReleasesScope}
        says, published in the GitHub repository the running build was
        published from, which it knows because that is baked into it. Only
        such a build updates itself. A build made anywhere else, as on a
        developer's machine, never looks for an update, never downloads one,
        and never replaces its binary, and the Updates section says why.

    checking:
        A check asks GitHub's releases API for the repository's releases,
        pre-releases included, and takes the one with the highest version
        `0.1.N`, comparing N as a number, never as text. It is newer only
        when its N is greater than the running build's; an older or equal one
        is never taken, so an update never goes back. A release without the
        asset for the running platform is passed over for the newest one
        that has it.

        Suspense checks a few seconds after it starts, and then every 6
        hours while it runs, in the background, never holding up anything
        else, and only while "Check for updates automatically" is on, as it
        is until turned off. That choice is remembered for the user, as the
        @{UserPreferencesScope} says. Check for updates, in the Updates
        section, checks straight away, whether it is on or not. A check that
        can't be made, as with no network or GitHub refusing it, is quiet
        when automatic, trying again at the next, and says why when asked
        for.

    downloading:
        A newer release found is downloaded straight away, in the
        background: the asset for the platform and architecture running,
        `suspense-0.1.N-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`, `suspense-0.1.N-windows-x86_64.zip`, or
        `suspense-0.1.N-macos-aarch64.tar.gz`. It is checked against the size
        GitHub gives for it, and against its SHA-256 digest where GitHub
        gives one, and one that doesn't match is thrown away and never used.
        The binary is taken out of the archive and staged beside the running
        binary, in the same directory, so it can be put in place by a rename,
        marked executable where the platform has such a mark. One download
        runs at a time; a newer release found while one is staged replaces
        it. A download that fails says so in the Updates section, and is
        tried again at the next check.

        Where the running binary's directory can't be written, nothing is
        downloaded: the Updates section says that Suspense can't update
        itself there, with the directory, and a link to the release's page,
        opened in the browser, so it can be updated by hand.

    restarting:
        Once an update is staged, a notification says "Suspense 0.1.N is
        ready", with a Restart button and a Later button. The Updates section
        says the same, with a Restart button, for as long as it stays staged.
        Later only closes the notification; the update stays staged, and is
        put in place whenever Suspense next quits.

        asking first while work is running, and doing nothing more if the
        quit is cancelled, then starts Suspense again from the same path once

        anything else, and takes effect at the launch after, the Updates
        section saying a restart finishes it.

        a step that fails puts back the binary that was there, and the
        Updates section says why it couldn't update.

content.text:
I've added a self-update spec: Suspense finds newer edge releases, downloads them in the background, and swaps in the new binary when it quits or restarts. `piton check` reports no problems, every changed file is formatted, and `piton build` succeeds. I confirmed the new scope and the Settings change in the refreshed reference.

**How it works:**
- **Which builds update:** only builds published by the edge-release workflow. Those builds now also bake in the repository they came from (`owner/name`). A build made anywhere else, such as a local `cargo run`, never checks, downloads or replaces itself.
- **Checking:**
  - It asks GitHub's releases API for the highest `0.1.N`, pre-releases included, comparing N as a number. It never goes back to an older version.
  - It checks a few seconds after launch and then every 6 hours, while "Check for updates automatically" is on. That's a new user preference, on by default.
  - Automatic checks fail quietly. A "Check for updates" you ask for says why it failed.
- **Downloading:**
  - It downloads the asset for the running platform and checks it against the size GitHub gives, and against the SHA-256 digest where GitHub gives one.
  - The binary is unpacked and staged in the same directory as the running binary, so a rename can put it in place.
  - If that directory isn't writable, nothing is downloaded. The Updates section says so and links to the release page.
- **Restarting:**
  - A notification says "Suspense 0.1.N is ready", with **Restart** and **Later**.
  - Restart quits the normal way, asking first if work is running, then relaunches.
  - Any quit puts a staged update in place. On Windows, the running binary is renamed aside first and deleted at the next launch.
  - An update left staged by a crash is put in place at the next launch and takes effect the launch after.
  - If a step fails, the old binary is put back.
- **Settings:** a new **Updates** section, after Containers, shows:
  - the running version
  - the "check automatically" checkbox and a Check for updates button
  - a status line: checking, up to date (with when it last checked), downloading, ready with a Restart button, or the error in red

**This run hit the same unowned-file error you showed me.** The build refused `.claude/reference/scope/edge-releases/index.md`, written by last turn's build. This container's `.piton` is still a temporary filesystem rather than the project's own folder, so the fix from two turns ago isn't in the code yet. I deleted the file, since it's generated reference output, and rebuilt cleanly.

Choices I made that you may want to change:
- **Timing:** it downloads automatically as soon as an update is found, and doesn't ask first.
- **Applying the update:** it happens on any quit, not only through the Restart button.
- **Signing:** none. It relies on HTTPS plus GitHub's size and digest, since the release binaries are unsigned.

## What changed in the spec, and the anchors the code should follow

- **New `spec/scope/self-update/index.pi` (`SelfUpdateScope`):**
  - **`SelfUpdateShape.description`:** only update when the build has a baked-in repository.
  - **`SelfUpdateShape.checking`:**
    - Use the GitHub releases API with pre-releases included, and pick the release with the highest numeric N that has this platform's asset.
    - Check at startup plus a few seconds, then every 6 hours, while the preference is on. The manual check ignores the preference.
    - Automatic failures are quiet; a manual check reports why.
  - **`SelfUpdateShape.downloading`:**
    - Download in the background, check size and the SHA-256 `digest` when present, and unpack `.tar.gz` or `.zip`.
    - Stage the binary in the executable's directory and mark it executable on Unix. Only one download runs at a time.
    - If the directory isn't writable, download nothing and show the directory and a link to the release page.
  - **`SelfUpdateShape.restarting`:**
    - Show the notification with Restart and Later.
    - Restart goes through the normal quit, including its confirmation, then relaunches from the same path.
    - On every quit, rename the staged binary into place. On Windows, rename the running binary aside first.
    - At launch, delete the set-aside binary and apply any update left staged.
    - If a swap fails, roll back. Any child process this starts follows `ApplicationShape.childProcesses`.
  - **`SelfUpdateShape.updatesSection`:** the Settings section's contents and status lines.
- **`EdgeReleasesShape.version`:** bake in the repository as well as the version, for example from `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` via `option_env!`.
- **`SettingsWindowShape.sidebar`:** add "Updates" after "Containers".
- **`UserPreferencesShape.preferences`:** add "check for updates automatically", which starts on.
- **`ApplicationShape.selfUpdate`:** links the new scope. No code needed for it.
